messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 23
- Gender: Female
- Ethnicity: South Asian
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: UX Designer
- Trauma Type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another
- Pcl5: 75

She is 23, South Asian, newly married, and works as a UX designer at a fast-growing startup where most days are spent thinking about user flows, edge cases, and how one small decision on a screen can send someone in the wrong direction. Before the accident, that way of thinking feels contained to work. Now it colors everything.

The event happens on a rainy weekday evening after she stays late to finish revisions for a product launch. Her husband has texted twice asking if she is on her way home. She remembers feeling rushed, distracted, and annoyed at herself for missing dinner again. At an intersection a few blocks from the office, she begins a left turn. Later, she will replay the exact sequence so many times that it feels more vivid than anything else in her life: the blur of headlights in the rain, the sudden shape of a motorbike coming through the intersection, the impossible thought — no, no, no — and then the impact.

The rider is thrown to the pavement. She is out of the car before it fully stops rolling. She remembers kneeling in the rain, hearing herself ask if he can hear her, hearing someone shout to call an ambulance, seeing blood near his leg at an angle that tells her something is terribly wrong. In the emergency department waiting area she sits soaked through, hands shaking uncontrollably, answering the same questions from police, from staff, from her husband when he arrives pale and breathless. She learns the rider survives but has multiple fractures and a serious head injury. Relief comes for a second and is immediately overtaken by something heavier: she did this. Someone else’s life is now split into before and after because of one movement of her hands.

In the first weeks, everyone around her speaks gently. Family members tell her it was an accident, that these things happen, that she should be grateful no one died. She nods, but inside she rejects every effort to soften it. At night she sees the rider’s body lifting from the bike just as she begins to fall asleep. When sleep comes, she wakes gasping, certain she has heard the thud again. She starts avoiding the route home, then avoids driving in rain, then driving at all. Her husband offers to take her to work, but even in the passenger seat she presses an invisible brake into the floor whenever a motorcycle appears beside them.

At work, the change is noticeable before she names it. She has always been thoughtful, a little perfectionistic in a way her team values. Now she cannot stop checking. She spends an hour debating the wording on a button because what if the user misunderstands, what if one confusing prompt causes damage, what if a tiny oversight becomes irreversible. In design reviews she goes quiet or apologizes excessively. If a colleague says, “No worries, we can fix it later,” she feels a jolt of panic. Later feels dangerous. Later is how terrible things happen. Her manager comments that she seems distracted. She begins missing details she would once have caught easily, then stays late trying to compensate, only to find herself frozen, staring at a prototype while the accident replays behind her eyes.

She does not tell many people the full story. In her community, news travels fast and shame travels faster. She imagines relatives lowering their voices about her, imagines being seen not as unlucky but careless, morally flawed. When her mother calls and says she sounds tired, she insists work is busy. With her husband, she is both clingier and more distant. She wants him near, especially at night, but recoils when he reaches for her after a nightmare because waking into touch feels, for a second, like waking back into impact. They begin arguing over small things — dishes, lateness, whether she has eaten — and both of them seem startled to realize the arguments are not about those things.

She carries guilt like a private ritual. She searches online for updates about road injuries and legal consequences. She checks the victim’s crowdfunding page more than once, donates anonymously, then feels disgusted with herself for imagining money means anything. Sometimes on her lunch break she sits in a stairwell and thinks that she should have been the one injured, that the wrong person walked away.

Months later, the world remains organized around threat and blame. Rain on the window makes her chest tighten. Sirens anywhere in the distance pull her instantly back to the intersection. She avoids certain streets, motorcycles, emergency dramas on television, even the smell of wet asphalt. When avoidance fails, she feels herself leave the present: her hearing narrows, her hands go cold, and she is once again standing in the road under streetlights, watching irreversible harm unfold in front of her.

What troubles her most is not only fear but the collapse of who she thought she was. She has always believed she is careful, responsible, someone others can trust. Now she studies herself as if she were a flawed product that caused injury in the field. She asks, over and over, what kind of person makes one mistake and changes another person’s life. Even on ordinary days, with her laptop open and her husband moving quietly around their apartment, some part of her is still at that intersection, waiting for the moment just before the turn, desperate to do it differently.
